text.p: A woman police officer was shot and badly wounded on Thursday in a suspected IRA guerrilla attack in Londonderry, Northern Ireland's second city.
Security sources said she was thought to have been shot from a passing vehicle while on guard duty at a security hut close to the city's courthouse.
The building is in the heart of the old walled city in a zone which is heavily protected by British forces following previous Irish Republican Army attacks.
The officer was hit in the chest and "her condition is serious," said a British security source.
A vehicle suspected to have been used in the incident was later found near the 400 year-old city walls leading to the Bogside, a Catholic Irish nationalist stronghold.
Security sources said the incident bore the hallmarks of an attack by the IRA, which is fighting a 28-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland.

Northern Ireland has been in a heightened state of tension over recent months amid growing hostilities by the IRA and several retaliatory attacks on Catholics by pro-British Loyalist guerrillas who are fighting to maintain British rule.

The IRA has killed two soldiers in the province since last October and carried out a series of mortar and gun ambushes. Late on Wednesday guerrillas sprayed two British military posts with gunfire on the border with the Irish republic in County Fermanagh.
Rumours surfaced in British and Irish media outlets on Thursday that the guerrillas might declare a 1600 GMT ceasefire but Sinn Fein, the IRA's political arm, poured cold water on the speculation.

On Wednesday Irish Prime Minister John Bruton launched a scathing attack on the guerrillas, saying that Catholics who vote for Sinn Fein in a May 1 British and Northern Ireland election would be casting a vote for violence.

Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams later repudiated Bruton's comments. He said Sinn Fein voters were supporting his party's so-called peace strategy which envisages Sinn Fein taking part in all-party talks and an end to all violence in the disputed province.
Britain and Ireland say that Sinn Fein will not get a seat in talks until the IRA abandons violence.
Northern Ireland's volatile political situation has become even more fragile in recent months with Loyalist guerrillas, loyal to Britain, targetting Catholics.

Loyalist commanders insist that a truce which they called in October 1994 is still in force, but Protestant extremists close to banned Loyalist guerrilla groups have been blamed for trying to kill a Catholic near Belfast on Wednesday and for murdering a Catholic man in the city in March.

The shooting in Londonderry happened hours after the end of the hearing of appeals by a number of republicans against convictions arising out of a riot which erupted when British Prime Minister John Major visited the city two years ago.
